_: Reference tables for block F: typical impacts of a strong eastern-type El Niño by region and season, food-import vulnerability, and what to do. Every row carries a source; a row without one must not reach the page. Impacts are TYPICAL, not guaranteed: the page says 'usually', never 'will'. Strength: robust (appears in most strong events) / likely (majority) / weak (some). Vulnerability 1–5: share of imports in cereal consumption and exposure of food-insecure populations, from FAO/World Bank reports.

sources.cpc: NOAA CPC, El Niño and La Niña: typical global impacts (warm-episode maps, DJF and JJA), cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/impacts
sources.iri: IRI, ENSO impacts by region and season, iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/enso
sources.giews: FAO GIEWS Special Alert 373, El Niño 2023–24: potential impacts on food security (Aug 2023)
sources.wfp: WFP, El Niño 2023–24 anticipatory action plans and regional outlooks
sources.nfidc: FAO / WTO list of Net Food-Importing Developing Countries; FAO cereal import dependency ratios (FAOSTAT food balances)
sources.wb: World Bank, Food Security Update (2024–2025), country import dependence
sources.ep: Eastern-Pacific (canonical) type: Rasmusson & Carpenter 1982; Ashok et al. 2007; coastal Peru impacts, SENAMHI/ENFEN bulletins

actions.drought: Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.
actions.flood: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early-warning for river basins.
actions.heat: Heat plans for cities and crops, irrigation scheduling, protection of vulnerable groups.
actions.import: Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.
actions.fisheries: Prepare for a collapse of coastal upwelling fisheries: fishing bans, income support, alternative supply of fish protein.
actions.none: No strong signal: watch the neighbours' harvests and world prices rather than local weather.

SON.note: Short rains (OND) usually well above normal; flooding and landslides, locust-friendly conditions.

DJF.note: Wet tail of the short rains into January.

MAM.note: Long rains show no consistent signal.

vulnerability.note: Large food-insecure population, cereal imports 20–40 % of consumption in Kenya and Somalia; floods hit pastoral and lowland cropping areas.

regions.name: Southern Africa
regions.countries: Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique, South Africa, Botswana, Namibia

SON.note: Late and weak start of the rainy season.

DJF.note: Main maize season drier and hotter than normal; 1982-83, 1991-92, 2015-16 and 2023-24 all brought regional maize failures.

MAM.note: Early end of rains; reduced harvest.

vulnerability.note: Maize-dependent diets, thin reserves; Zimbabwe, Malawi and Zambia declared drought emergencies in 2024.

SON.note: No consistent signal for the second rainy season.

MAM.note: Weak, mixed signal at the start of the first rainy season.

vulnerability.note: Rice and wheat imports matter (Nigeria, Ghana); the exposure is through world prices rather than local weather.

regions.name: Sahel
regions.countries: Mali, Niger, Chad, Burkina Faso, Senegal, Sudan

SON.note: Rainy season (JAS) tends to be weaker in El Niño years; the 2026 season is mostly over, the effect is on the harvest already in the ground.

vulnerability.note: Highest structural food insecurity, conflict, cereal imports 30–60 % of consumption in Mauritania, Senegal; any price shock is a crisis.

regions.name: Middle East and North Africa
regions.countries: Egypt, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Yemen, Iraq, Iran, Gulf states

DJF.note: Eastern Mediterranean and Gulf winters tend to be wetter; north-west Africa mixed.

MAM.note: Weak wet tendency in the Middle East.

vulnerability.note: The world's largest wheat importers: Egypt, Algeria, Morocco, Yemen, Saudi Arabia import 50–100 % of cereals; exposure is almost entirely through world prices and exporters' harvests.

regions.name: South Asia
regions.countries: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal

SON.note: Monsoon withdrawal earlier; post-monsoon (NE monsoon) mixed, Sri Lanka and south India often wetter.

DJF.note: Warmer, drier winter in north India and Pakistan; rabi wheat at risk from March heat.

vulnerability.note: Largely self-sufficient in cereals but a huge population close to the margin; India restricts exports in bad years, which moves world rice prices.

regions.name: Southeast Asia and Indonesia
regions.countries: Indonesia, Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Papua New Guinea

SON.note: Delayed monsoon onset, drought and peat fires in Indonesia and Malaysia; Philippines dry.

DJF.note: Reduced rainfall persists; rice and palm-oil yields fall; Philippine drought.

MAM.note: Dry tail; reservoirs low, hydropower reduced.

vulnerability.note: Rice self-sufficiency thin in Indonesia and the Philippines (both import in El Niño years); Thailand and Vietnam are exporters whose smaller crops raise world prices.

SON.note: Southern China somewhat wetter in autumn.

DJF.note: Wetter winter in southern China; milder winter in Japan and Korea.

MAM.note: Wetter spring in south China; the following summer often brings Yangtze flooding (1998, 2016).

vulnerability.note: China holds large reserves but is the largest soybean and a major maize importer; Japan and Korea import most cereals but are wealthy.

SON.note: Spring drier and hotter in the east and north; winter-crop finishing affected; bushfire season starts early.

DJF.note: Hot, dry summer in the east; bushfires; northern wet season delayed.

vulnerability.note: Major wheat exporter: a poor Australian crop tightens the world wheat balance and raises prices for importers elsewhere.

regions.name: Pacific Islands
regions.countries: Fiji, Papua New Guinea highlands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Tuvalu, Micronesia

SON.note: Western Pacific (PNG, Fiji, Vanuatu) drier, central Pacific (Kiribati, Tuvalu) much wetter; sea level drops in the west, exposing reefs.

DJF.note: Drought in the west persists; tropical cyclone activity shifts east towards French Polynesia and the Cooks.

vulnerability.note: Small islands import most staples and depend on shipping; the 1997-98 event brought famine conditions to the PNG highlands.

SON.note: Weak signals in autumn; hurricane season in the Atlantic usually suppressed.

DJF.note: Wetter southern tier from California to Florida; warmer and drier in the northern US and Canada; Pacific North-west and Ohio valley drier.

MAM.note: Wet spring in the southern Plains and Gulf; good for winter wheat.

vulnerability.note: Largest maize and soybean exporter; El Niño winters are usually favourable for US crops, which eases world supply.

regions.name: Central America and the Caribbean
regions.countries: Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Haiti, Cuba, Dominican Republic

SON.note: Dry corridor (Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua) drier; second bean and maize crop (postrera) at risk.

MAM.note: Late start of the first rainy season (primera).

vulnerability.note: Haiti and the dry-corridor countries combine high import dependence with chronic food insecurity and out-migration.

SON.note: Coastal Ecuador and northern Peru begin to see heavy rain; 'coastal El Niño' effect strongest in eastern-type events.

DJF.note: Torrential rain and floods on the Peruvian and Ecuadorian coast (1982-83, 1997-98, 2017); anchoveta fishery collapses; Bolivian altiplano and southern Peruvian Andes drier.

MAM.note: Coastal floods persist through the southern-hemisphere autumn; landslides; disease outbreaks.

vulnerability.note: Peru imports wheat and maize; fishmeal exports and coastal agriculture (rice, mango, asparagus) are hit directly; Colombia and Bolivia rely on imports of wheat.

regions.name: Southern Cone
regions.countries: southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, northern Argentina; north-east Brazil

SON.note: Southern Brazil, Uruguay and north-east Argentina wetter; floods in the Paraná basin; north-east Brazil drier.

DJF.note: Wet summer favourable for Argentine soybean and maize once floods drain; north-east Brazil drought.

vulnerability.note: Net exporters of soybean, maize and wheat; the world-price effect is usually favourable (bigger crops), the local risk is floods and the north-east drought.
